reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A mature, encapsulated collection of necrotic pancreatic and peripancreatic tissue that develops typically about four weeks after an episode of necrotising pancreatitis
Distinguished from a pseudocyst by its heterogeneous content, which includes solid debris rather than pure fluid, under the revised Atlanta classification
May be sterile or become infected; infected necrosis is suggested by clinical deterioration, sepsis, or gas within the collection on imaging
Contrast-enhanced CT shows an encapsulated collection with variable solid and liquid components in or around the pancreas
Asymptomatic sterile collections can be managed conservatively, as many resolve or remain stable without intervention
When drainage is needed, a step-up approach is favoured, beginning with percutaneous or endoscopic drainage before escalating to minimally invasive necrosectomy
Endoscopic transmural drainage with lumen-apposing metal stents and, where required, direct endoscopic necrosectomy has become a mainstay of management
reference.pathophysiology: Walled-off pancreatic necrosis is a late local complication of necrotising pancreatitis. During the acute illness, ischaemic and enzymatic injury produces necrosis of pancreatic parenchyma and surrounding fat, generating an acute necrotic collection containing both liquefied and solid material. Over the following weeks a fibrous and granulation-tissue wall matures around this collection, converting it into an organised, encapsulated cavity that still contains devitalised solid debris. The retained necrotic tissue can become secondarily infected by gut-derived organisms, and the collection may erode adjacent structures, obstruct the stomach or duodenum, compress the bile duct, or communicate with the pancreatic duct, producing persistent leakage.
additionalDifferentials: Acute necrotic collection (before maturation of the wall)
Duodenal or gastric outlet obstruction from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT to define the extent, wall maturity, and solid content of the collection
MRI or endoscopic ultrasound to better characterise solid debris and guide drainage
Inflammatory markers and blood cultures if infection is suspected
Image-guided aspiration for culture when infected necrosis is in question
Assessment of pancreatic duct integrity (for example MRCP) to detect disconnected duct syndrome
Monitoring of nutritional status and glycaemic control
redFlags: Clinical deterioration, persistent fever, or sepsis suggesting infected necrosis
Gas within the collection on imaging
Gastric outlet or biliary obstruction from mass effect
Haemorrhage into the collection or a pseudoaneurysm of a splanchnic vessel
reference.prognosis: Sterile, asymptomatic collections often resolve or stabilise without intervention and carry a good outlook; infected necrosis substantially increases morbidity and mortality, though outcomes have improved with a minimally invasive step-up strategy and delayed intervention where possible.
pitfalls: Intervening too early before the wall has matured, which increases complications
Mistaking walled-off necrosis for a simple pseudocyst and attempting drainage of solid debris through inadequate routes
Overlooking a disconnected pancreatic duct, which predisposes to persistent or recurrent collections
Failing to recognise vascular complications such as pseudoaneurysm before drainage
Delaying antibiotics and source control once infection is established
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Revised Atlanta classification of acute pancreatitis
Guidelines on the step-up management of necrotising pancreatitis
management: Manage sterile, asymptomatic collections conservatively, as many resolve or remain stable, while supporting nutrition preferably by the enteral route and optimising glycaemic control
Delay any intervention where possible until the collection wall has matured, which reduces procedural morbidity
Treat infected or symptomatic necrosis with a step-up approach, beginning with endoscopic ultrasound-guided transmural drainage or percutaneous catheter drainage
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics with good pancreatic penetration, such as a carbapenem, for confirmed or strongly suspected infected necrosis
Escalate to minimally invasive necrosectomy, whether endoscopic or video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement, when drainage alone fails to control sepsis
Identify and manage disconnected pancreatic duct syndrome and treat local complications such as gastric outlet or biliary obstruction and haemorrhage
Coordinate care through a hepatobiliary and pancreatology multidisciplinary team with interventional radiology and therapeutic endoscopy
